questions.q: Why do real quantum processors only natively implement a small, fixed set of gates rather than every gate used in circuit design?
options: Each native gate requires its own precisely engineered control sequence, so implementing many gates natively multiplies hardware difficulty; a small universal set is enough to reach everything else through composition
Hardware is physically incapable of ever applying more than one type of gate to a qubit
Non-native gates are purely theoretical constructs with no physical realization possible on any hardware
Using more native gates would violate the normalization requirement on quantum states
questions.explain: The constraint is engineering difficulty, not physical impossibility — each native gate needs its own tuned control pulse. The universality result is what makes a small native set sufficient: everything else can be built from it.

questions.q: What does it mean for a gate set like {H, T, CNOT} to be 'universal'?
options: Any quantum circuit can be approximated to arbitrary precision using only gates drawn from that set
The set contains literally every gate that any quantum circuit could ever use
The gates in the set can only be applied to one specific qubit at a time
The set works only for circuits with exactly 2 qubits
questions.explain: Universal means sufficient-by-approximation: any circuit, however it was originally specified, can be rewritten using only gates from a universal set, to any desired precision — not that the set already contains every gate.

questions.q: Multiplying the T gate's matrix by itself (T·T), what result does the computation give for the bottom-right entry, and what gate does this match?
options: Exactly i (real part 0, imaginary part 1), matching the S gate's bottom-right entry
Exactly -1, matching the Z gate's bottom-right entry
Approximately but not exactly i, since T·T can only approximate S
Exactly 1, meaning T·T has no effect at all, equivalent to the identity gate
questions.explain: Squaring T's phase factor e^(iπ/4) gives e^(iπ/2), which equals exactly i — not an approximation. Computing it via complex [real,imag] multiplication confirms the real part is exactly 0 and the imaginary part is exactly 1, matching S = [[1,0],[0,i]] exactly.

questions.q: What role does CNOT specifically play within a universal gate set like {H, T, CNOT}?
options: It supplies the entangling, multi-qubit power that no combination of single-qubit gates (like H and T alone) could ever produce
It is only included for convenience and could be removed without affecting universality
It replaces the need for H and T entirely once enough CNOT gates are chained together
It is the gate responsible for approximating arbitrary single-qubit rotations
questions.explain: H and T (long sequences of them) can approximate arbitrary single-qubit rotations, but single-qubit gates alone can never entangle qubits. CNOT is what supplies the entangling power; together, single-qubit universality plus CNOT is enough to reach any circuit.

questions.q: Why can the same logical circuit end up with very different real depth or gate count when run on two different quantum processors?
options: A compiler/transpiler rewrites each logical gate into that specific hardware's native gate set, and different hardware has different native gates, so the same logical gate may take one native operation on one device and several on another
Logical circuits are randomly reassigned different gates each time they are compiled, regardless of hardware
Different hardware platforms use entirely different mathematical rules for quantum mechanics
Depth and gate count are fixed properties of the algorithm and never change regardless of hardware
questions.explain: Decomposition is hardware-specific: a gate your circuit uses at the logical level might be one device's native gate (one operation) but require a multi-gate rewrite on another device with a different native set — directly changing the real depth and gate count.
